Hand-edit here, then re-run scripts/render-leader-handouts.mjs.

1.title: Unit 1, Lesson 1: Apologetics
1.bigIdea: Apologetics comes from the Greek apologia in 1 Peter 3:15: giving a reasoned defense for the hope we have, with gentleness and respect. This year asks students, and you, to know why you believe what you believe and to discuss it intelligently.
keyPoints: Peter commands believers to be prepared to give a reason, a courtroom-style defense, for their faith; that word apologia is where apologetics comes from.
Peter wrote to Christians persecuted by Rome, and that same responsibility to stand and defend belief applies to us today.
Being called to give a defense also means being capable of one; Peter in Acts 4:20 could not stop speaking of what he had seen and heard.
Some cite 1 Corinthians 2 to claim persuasion is dangerous, but in context Paul is not forbidding reasoned evidence; Jesus, Paul, and Peter all gave good reasons.
Create an environment where students can ask anything, even questions that voice doubt, and feel safe doing it.
You do not need every answer; saying 'let's figure this out together' builds the relationship and finds the answer, using church, seminary, and Awana resources.

forYou: Why do you believe what you believe, and can you discuss those beliefs intelligently?
Do your students feel free to ask any question, including ones that voice doubt? What would make it safer?
How will you respond when a student asks something you cannot answer?
What resources or people could you draw on this year when hard questions come up?

2.title: Unit 1, Lesson 2: Faith
2.bigIdea: Biblical faith is not wandering in the darkness hoping you are right. John says the miraculous signs were written so we may believe: faith is trust based on evidence, and like any relationship, the more reasons we have to trust Christ, the deeper the relationship goes.
keyPoints: The speaker once saw faith as stumbling in the dark, like breaking his toe in a pitch-black apartment, and many students still see it that way.
John 20:30-31 says the recorded signs were written so you may believe; John gives seven escalating signs, plus the resurrection, as reasons to believe.
Biblical faith is trust based on evidence, and just as trust deepens human relationships, knowing Christ better deepens our relationship with him.
Hebrews 11:1's 'certain' carries the idea of a foundation or substructure, like a basement so solid you never fear the house will cave in.
Jesus kept his wounds after the resurrection, showing them to Thomas as one more reason to believe he did exactly what he said.
Create space for students to consider the evidence themselves, so faith becomes their own rather than borrowed from parents or leaders; that faith sticks through college.

forYou: Do you have your own faith, or are you still believing what your parents or others told you to believe?
Have you considered the evidence God has given for who Jesus is? Is it enough?
How does trust between friends grow, and how is that like trusting Christ?
How can we help students move from accepting what we tell them to discovering it is true?

3.title: Unit 1, Lesson 3: Truth
3.bigIdea: Students live in a post-truth, relativist culture that says you can create your own reality. But truth is what corresponds with reality, independent of anyone's opinion. Jesus' claim in John 14 is objective, either true or false, and understanding that leads students to genuine freedom in Christ.
keyPoints: Oxford's 2016 word of the year, 'post-truth,' captures the relativism students face daily: feelings and personal belief outweighing objective facts.
When leaders present something as objectively true, students often hear only 'that's what you think,' a wall this lesson helps take down.
Nothing else this year, Scripture's authority, the resurrection, God's existence, the problem of evil, can be discussed until students understand the nature of truth.
Truth is what corresponds with reality, and coherence or practicality is not enough: Santa Claus makes sense to kids but does not line up with reality.
Subjective truths, like a favorite ice cream flavor, are about the subject's experience; objective truths, like a shirt's color, hold regardless of anyone's opinion.
Culture lumps Jesus with subjective truth, but John 14's 'I am the way' is an objective claim: if true, contradicting beliefs are false.

forYou: What is the difference between a subjective truth and an objective truth? Give an example of each.
Why do people put belief in Jesus on the subjective side, and why does John 14 not allow that?
Can something make sense and be practical but still not be true? How would you tell?
How does truth open the door to a life of genuine freedom in Christ?

4.title: Unit 1, Lesson 4: Logic
4.bigIdea: Scripture treats logic as a vital tool, not a threat: Hebrews calls believers past milk to maturity, Jesus commands loving God with all our mind and models logical argument himself. Students should embrace clear, careful thinking as part of their search for truth, so they can look truth in the face and see Jesus.
keyPoints: Hebrews 5-6 urges believers to move from spiritual milk to solid food and maturity; Peter and Paul echo the call to renewed, Christ-like minds.
Jesus said to worship God with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength, so logic has a clear place in faith.
Reductio ad absurdum means drawing an argument to its absurd conclusion, like a dad answering 'all my friends did it' with the jumping-off-a-bridge reply.
In Matthew 22 Jesus uses that same logical analysis in his confrontation with the Pharisees.
Throughout Acts, in Corinth, Ephesus, Thessalonica, and Athens, Paul constantly reasons from the Scriptures to show who Jesus is.
Some arguments against Christianity sound good, so discuss them honestly, gauging what your students are ready to handle before diving in.

forYou: Should faith make sense? What parts of faith seem confusing until you think them through?
What about your faith does not make sense to you, and what would it take to work through it?
How do you already use logic in your relationships to figure out what is true?
What is an argument against Christianity that sounds good, and does it hold up logically?

5.title: Unit 2, Lesson 1: Worldview
5.bigIdea: A worldview is the set of lenses through which we see and interpret the world, shaping how we answer life's foundational questions and how we live. Students will compare naturalism, pantheism, and monotheism; leaders should not assume students already hold a biblical worldview, and should be patient as change comes slowly.
keyPoints: Like the speaker's first pair of glasses, a worldview changes everything you see; it is foundational, life-shaping questions about reality that dictate how you live.
Students will examine other popular lenses, naturalism and pantheism, then monotheism, because those views reach them through movies, music, art, TV, and books.
Do not assume your students have a biblical worldview; even churched kids often hold a 'buffet' worldview assembled from whatever looked good online.
The four worldview questions gently draw out what students think and reveal flaws in their thinking, so encourage honest answers, not expected ones.
Worldviews must be coherent and consistent; the buffet approach eventually fails, and Christianity is compelling because it is entirely coherent and consistent.
Do not expect students to change worldviews right away; changing how you see reality is a huge, anxious adjustment, so be patient and walk alongside them.

forYou: What lenses are you already looking through, and where did they come from?
Where might your own worldview be a 'buffet,' with pieces that do not fit together?
How do movies, music, and media communicate naturalism or pantheism to you without saying so?
Is your group a place where students answer honestly rather than saying what leaders want to hear? How can you tell?

6.title: Unit 2, Lesson 2: Monotheism
6.bigIdea: Monotheism is more than the claim that one God exists: it is the view that a single, personal, all-powerful Creator has made himself known. In Exodus 6 God reveals himself to Moses as Yahweh, a covenant-remembering, redeeming God who pursues his creation, which sets up everything Christianity will claim.
keyPoints: In Exodus 6 God tells Moses that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob knew him as God Almighty, but not by his name, the Lord.
The name Yahweh, 'I am who I am,' reveals God's personal nature, his holiness, and a covenant becoming more real than before.
Having covered naturalism (the West) and pantheism (the East), the case for Christianity must first show a single, personal, all-powerful Creator exists.
Monotheism is a worldview containing Judaism, Christianity, and Islam; it means leaving the buffet and ordering the most consistent, coherent dish off the menu.
God is not a creator who walks away; he is actively engaged in history, redeeming and chasing after his image-bearers even after we screwed it up.
That personal, pursuing God sets up what Jesus does, the Holy Spirit, and the Trinity; coming weeks build the case that Christianity within monotheism is true.

forYou: What changes between knowing God as 'God Almighty' and knowing him by name as Yahweh?
What would it look like to view the world as if one personal God cares about and pursues you individually?
How would a monotheistic worldview change your thoughts on morality, justice, love, and how you act at school?
How could Christians looking through this lens actually influence the culture, rather than just being influenced by it?

7.title: Unit 2, Lesson 3: Pantheism
7.bigIdea: Pantheism, the main worldview of the East, says god is in everything and is everything, with no line between Creator and creation. Its ideas reach students through karma, meditation, yoga and Star Wars, and losing that line leads straight back to idolatry.
keyPoints: Pantheism dominates Eastern thought, yet karma, meditation, yoga and Star Wars’ “force” show it has reached the West, so students need to learn to recognize it.
It teaches that god is literally part of everything, rocks, trees, all of nature, a divine spark or force; that is not the same as the Holy Spirit dwelling in believers.
The key word is distinction: naturalism says there is no God, while pantheism says God exists but is not distinct from anything that is created.
At the Areopagus, Paul helps Stoics, who believed much like today’s pantheists, see that God is personal and near yet distinct from and other than us.
Without distinction, rocks and trees are as divine as God, so worshiping them is no different; losing it leads back to the root of sin, idolatry.
Teach this in love, never mocking other worldviews; a God who is distinct, holy and other than us gives a standard for right and wrong, just and unjust.

forYou: Where might you treat creation, a person or yourself as something close to divine, even in small ways?
How does God being completely other than you shape the way you decide what is right and wrong?
Could a skeptical student hear you describe another worldview without feeling mocked? What would help?
forGroup: In your own words, what does pantheism say about God, and how is that different from the Holy Spirit living in a believer?
Where have you seen ideas like karma, “the force” or a divine spark in movies, music or wellness trends?
Why does it matter whether God is distinct from creation? What changes if he isn’t?
What things get treated as if they were divine in our culture, and what does that look like at your school?
How could you talk with a friend who holds another worldview so they feel respected, not made fun of?

8.title: Unit 2, Lesson 4: Naturalism
8.bigIdea: Naturalism, the dominant worldview of the West, says only what our five senses can detect is real and that science alone must supply life’s meaning. But it cannot answer why we exist or account for justice, love and morality, and without God, as Ecclesiastes says, everything is meaningless.
keyPoints: Naturalism says only what the five senses can detect makes up reality; students meet it every day, especially in science, math and technology classes.
It claims any meaning in life must come through science, but science only reaches the natural world; the goal is for students to see naturalism can’t work.
Closely tied to atheism, it can’t explain how the universe came to be or why; the “why” question can be asked again and again without an answer.
Justice, love and morality can’t be touched or tasted, yet some morals hold for all cultures and all time, so they demand a deeper explanation.
Solomon opens Ecclesiastes with “meaningless, meaningless”: without God putting meaning in life, all our labor and effort comes to nothing.
Rejecting God while caring for orphans, widows and clean water is inconsistent; that sense of justice points beyond nature to a Creator God.

forYou: Where does an “only what I can see counts” mindset creep into how you think or live during the week?
Why do you care about justice and love, and how would you explain that to someone who doesn’t believe in God?
How can you let the discussion flow freely while still gently challenging students’ thinking?
forGroup: In your own words, what does naturalism say is real, and where does it say meaning comes from?
Where do you see naturalism show up in your classes or at school, beyond evolution?
If only the natural world exists, where do justice, love and right and wrong come from?
Why do people who don’t believe in God still care about clean water or helping others? What might that point to?
What gives your work and effort meaning, and how would your answer change without God?

9.title: Unit 3, Lesson 1: Science
9.bigIdea: Students are often taught that faith and science belong in separate worlds. They don’t: the more we discover through science, the more we see how awesome God is, and science lays a foundation for understanding our world instead of contradicting our faith.
keyPoints: You don’t need to be a science expert. Students are widely taught that faith and science don’t belong together; the speaker’s own teacher drew that line back in seventh grade.
As STEM studies and careers grow more popular, that split will only sharpen. Students need to see the two worlds connect: discovering more through science means discovering more of God.
Don’t try to master all the science yourself. Instead, find the students who love science, math or technology and get them engaged now.
Make the storyteller the centerpiece this week: someone from your church who works in the sciences. Talk with them first; even Christian teachers can struggle to make the connection.
Beyond the provided questions, ask students what they’re studying in school, even bring textbooks. Let them teach you while you help them see the biblical worldview behind it.
We often live in a two-story house: Jesus kept upstairs in the private sphere, school and work downstairs in public. The goal is to bring Jesus into the public space.

forYou: Where do I keep my faith upstairs, separate from my work or public life?
Who in our church could tell students how they see God in their scientific work?
What would help me lead a science unit with confidence, even without being an expert?
forGroup: What are you studying in science or math right now, and how might it connect to what you believe about God?
Have you ever been told faith and science don’t belong together? How did that land with you?
What’s something about the natural world that makes you wonder who, or what, is behind it?
Where do you find it easiest, and hardest, to bring your faith into school or work?
What questions about science and faith would you most like this unit to answer?

10.title: Unit 3, Lesson 2: Universe
10.bigIdea: Genesis tells us God designed the world, and nature says the same thing: the earth is fine-tuned, set just so for life to survive and thrive. That fine-tuning shows more than a God who exists; it shows a God who lovingly made a home for us.
keyPoints: The bottle flip looks like pure luck, but it’s really fine-tuning: the right bottle, the right amount of water and the right spin make it land every time.
Genesis tells us God created and designed the world. But even without Scripture, nature itself tells us the same thing about God’s design.
The atmosphere, the earth’s rotation and its distance from the sun are set just so for life. Is that random chance, or a well-crafted design by God?
Did the universe just restart over and over until it worked, like flipping a bottle enough times? This lesson looks for real design behind the conditions for life.
This week’s one word is thinking. Last week said science furthers faith; now students start putting the pieces together for themselves.
Fine-tuning shows more than a habitable planet: God made a home for us, with his heart and love in mind. Ask what that says about his character.

forYou: What does the care built into creation tell me about God’s character?
Which parts of the natural world do I take for granted that I could stop and consider this week?
How can I help students think the pieces through, not just hear the conclusions?
forGroup: What did the bottle flip show you about the difference between luck and fine-tuning?
If you didn’t have the Bible, what could nature alone tell you about whether there’s a designer?
Which seems harder for you to believe, random chance or design, and why?
What does it mean to you that God made the earth a home, not just a place to survive?
What questions about the universe and God are you still working through?

11.title: Unit 3, Lesson 3: DNA
11.bigIdea: Halfway through the science unit, pause and take stock of your relationships and of how well students are really following. Slow down where you need to, and use the provided misconceptions and simple examples to make hard ideas clear.
keyPoints: Check your relationships: are you building a culture where questions are welcome, students are honest with you and each other, and faith is growing?
Notice whether those relationships are deepening, whether new students are coming in, and how well they’re fitting in.
Ask how students are tracking. Some nod along without getting it, some are fired up and asking great questions, and many are somewhere in between.
Don’t be afraid to slow down, adapt and revisit concepts. Don’t move forward until you’re sure your students are ready.
The provided misconceptions are a window into the narrative students meet in their school textbooks, even if not in those exact words.
Choose examples that simplify hard ideas. The best one is Sean’s simple description of a book to help us understand DNA.

forYou: How are my relationships with students really going, and who have I lost track of?
Where might my students be nodding along without truly understanding?
Which concept from this unit do I need to slow down and revisit before moving on?
forGroup: How did comparing DNA to a book help you understand it, and what still feels unclear?
What have you been taught in school about where DNA and life came from?
Which part of this science unit has made the most sense to you so far, and which the least?
What questions about science and faith do you still have that we haven’t covered?
What would make it easier for you to ask honest questions in this group?

12.title: Unit 3, Lesson 4: Designer
12.bigIdea: Science doesn’t contradict faith: fine-tuning, DNA and design all give evidence for God. As the creation and evolution conversation comes alive, help eager students speak in truth and love, and give unsure students room to ask for more.
keyPoints: Recap: science is a foundation for understanding our world, not a contradiction of faith, and fine-tuning, DNA and design each point to God.
Keep two kinds of students in mind this week. Design is where the conversation between creation and evolution really comes alive.
Some students will be fired up to argue with teachers who likely know more than they do. Champion them, but coach them to speak in truth and love.
Challenging teachers and classmates is okay when done with appropriate respect, especially toward teachers, and in the right kinds of conversations.
Other students are still unsure. Take inventory with them plainly: was this enough evidence, do they need more, and what questions remain?
The goal is a deep conviction about what they believe and why, shared relationally with love and humility. Help eager students be patient; there’s more to learn.

forYou: When I’m eager to win an argument, does my tone still show truth and love?
Which unsure student could I take inventory with one-on-one this week?
How well can I explain why I believe, not just what I believe?
forGroup: Of fine-tuning, DNA and design, which evidence for God seems strongest to you, and why?
What would you still need to see or hear to feel more sure about any of this?
If a teacher disagreed with you about creation, how could you respond with respect?
What’s the difference between winning an argument and having a good conversation?
What questions or clarifications would help you most right now?

13.title: Unit 4, Lesson 1: Morality
13.bigIdea: Many students are taught that right and wrong are just opinions, so when we teach morality they may hear only our opinion. But we can’t measure ourselves by ourselves: our sense of right and wrong needs a standard beyond us, and it points us to God.
keyPoints: Morality seems simple, but students are often taught that moral claims are opinion. When we speak about truth, some hear only what we happen to think.
Meet with your small group leaders: talk through what they may hear, and gather students’ views on right and wrong. Some answers may surprise you.
As a teacher, the speaker found students copying homework in the hallway. Asked whether it was wrong, they simply said no, with no reason given.
Schools often label anything about feelings or beliefs as opinion, and that slope runs from copying homework to equality, murder and marriage.
Little Johnny measured himself as “one Johnny tall.” We can’t measure ourselves by ourselves; morality needs an external standard, and that points to God.
Respond with grace and love and truly listen, learn where their ideas come from, then challenge their thinking with care. Share this with your small group leaders.

forYou: Where do I present my views as obvious fact without explaining where my morals come from?
How do I react when a student pushes back, and can I listen without taking offense?
What do my small group leaders need to hear from me before this week’s discussions?
forGroup: What’s the difference between a fact and an opinion when it comes to right and wrong?
Where do most of your ideas about right and wrong come from: school, home, online or media?
Is anything wrong for everyone, everywhere, no matter what they think? How would you know?
What did the “one Johnny tall” story show you about needing a standard beyond ourselves?
When you disagree with someone about right and wrong, how can you listen well and still be honest?

14.title: Unit 4, Lesson 2: Beauty
14.bigIdea: Beauty, agency and story may seem lighter than earlier lessons, but they’re important pointers to God in students’ everyday lives. Use this week to step back and evaluate where each student is, so you can wisely shape the second half of the year.
keyPoints: Don’t rush beauty, agency and story because they seem strange. They’re important pointers to God in the things students see and touch every day.
Ask where each student is now: revisit the questions, thoughts and beliefs they came in with and any notes you took. What has changed, good or bad?
Keep a few Essentials books on hand for new students, and learn whether newcomers are seekers, skeptics or church kids who just moved.
Watch for recurring questions. Students, especially inquisitive ones, often can’t move on until a question is answered, so pause and answer it head on.
Don’t focus only on engaged students or on one skeptic. Talk one-on-one with the student who isn’t buying it, and don’t forget everyone in the middle.
Decide how to move forward: keep going, or pause and revisit a lesson. The goal is students prepared to move the gospel forward and proclaim the kingdom.

forYou: Which students have changed since the start of the year, and which haven’t?
Do I focus on the engaged students or on one skeptic, and who in the middle am I missing?
What recurring question do I need to stop and answer head on?
forGroup: Where have you noticed something beautiful this week, and what did it make you think or feel?
Why do you think people everywhere are drawn to beauty?
How might beauty in everyday life point to God, and why might it not convince someone?
What question from this year still feels unanswered for you?
Looking back on the year so far, what has changed in how you think about faith?

15.title: Unit 4, Lesson 3: Agency
15.bigIdea: Our ability to choose is a privilege and a responsibility God has given us: free will points to him, and how we use it should reflect him. This week, also take your community’s temperature, checking that every student feels loved, challenged and safe.
keyPoints: Choices govern so much of life, from instant decisions to hard ones. They’re a privilege and a responsibility from God, and another pointer to him.
Nail down two things with students: our free will points to God, and our free will should reflect him in how we live as Christians.
Last week you took your students’ temperature; now take your community’s. Does every student feel they belong and can share what they think?
Are leaders building an atmosphere of discussion where questions are welcome, grace and truth go together, no one dominates and everyone is invited in?
Love students and challenge them; don’t confuse love with letting them think whatever they want. In the speaker’s experience, the most challenged felt most loved.
Do students feel safe to be honest, and do small groups serve one another? Serve together in the community. With exams near, use fun games to show choices’ power.

forYou: Do I confuse loving students with simply letting them think what they want?
Which student has great things to say but doesn’t feel safe saying them?
How do my own choices this week reflect who God is?
forGroup: Why do you think God gave people the ability to choose at all?
How could having free will be a pointer to God?
What’s a recent choice, big or small, that showed what you really value?
What makes a choice reflect God, and what makes it not?
What would make this group a place where you can be completely honest?

16.title: Unit 4, Lesson 4: Story
16.bigIdea: We love great stories because we bear the image of God, the source of story itself, and that is another pointer to him. Now halfway through the curriculum, take a simple midterm: have students teach back what they’ve learned, and look honestly at where you got stuck.
keyPoints: Students need to see that story comes from God. We can tell great stories because we reflect his image, another pointer that he exists.
Look for redemptive and salvation themes in stories: your own, students’, someone you know, a book or a movie. Many stories carry biblical themes.
You’re officially halfway through the curriculum, so evaluate how the year is going. Call it your midterm, with two simple suggestions.
First, have students pick a favorite lesson or topic and teach it back or lead a discussion. If they can communicate it accurately, they’ve got it.
Second, look at where you got stuck: research more, find another video, or bring in an apologetics expert from the list at AwanaYM.org.
If you’re struggling, reach out by email, Twitter or Facebook. The In Two Minutes videos for students invite further questions in their comments.

forYou: Which topic from the first half left me least comfortable, and what would help?
Which students could I invite to teach a lesson back to the group?
Where in my own story can I see God’s redemption at work?
forGroup: What’s a favorite movie or book of yours, and where do you see redemption in its story?
Why do you think people everywhere love telling and hearing stories?
How could our love of story point to God, and what makes that hard to accept?
Which lesson from this year could you teach back to the group, and what would you say?
Where have you seen something broken in your own life turn into something good?

17.title: Unit 5, Lesson 1: Miracles
17.bigIdea: Miracles are less something to prove than signposts: because miracles happen, they point to the God who acts. This week helps students define a real miracle, weigh what science can and can’t explain, and consider that God can still work miracles today.
keyPoints: The aim isn’t only to prove miracles exist but to show they point to God; 1 Kings 18, Elijah and the prophets of Baal, puts God’s sovereign power on display.
The intro experience asks for the most improbable event in history, so students can tell a biblical miracle from a lucky parking spot or the “miracle of birth.”
For a storyteller, consider a trusted student who has witnessed something like a healing; the speaker recalls a student whose mission-trip experience shaped her life.
Students are conditioned to assume science explains everything. Keep a healthy balance: some things can be explained, but science can’t explain the supernatural.
Expect “Why don’t I see miracles like the lame man Peter and John healed?” We can’t say they don’t happen today; God still has the power to do them.
In small groups, note who is convinced miracles are possible and have happened, ask what it would take, and walk gently with anyone asking why God healed someone else.

forYou: Do I tend to explain things away before I consider that God might be at work?
Where have I seen God act in a way I couldn’t explain, and have I told anyone about it?
How will I respond when a student asks why God healed someone else but not them?
forGroup: How would you define a miracle, and how is it different from something that’s just unlikely or lucky?
What do you think science can explain, and where do you think its explanations stop?
What would it take for you to be convinced that miracles are possible today?
Have you or someone you know experienced something you’d call a miracle? What made it feel that way?
If God can do miracles, how do you make sense of the times He doesn’t seem to?

18.title: Unit 5, Lesson 2: Resurrection
18.bigIdea: Without the resurrection, Christianity falls apart, and the resurrection can be examined as a real historical event. The evidence for it outweighs every rival explanation, so the bigger question for students is what changes if they’re convinced.
keyPoints: In 1 Corinthians 15, Paul makes the resurrection the thread everything hangs on; many church kids know Jesus rose but have never heard there’s historical evidence for it.
Mainline history agrees Jesus lived, was crucified by the Romans and buried; Paul names witnesses, the twelve and more than 500 people, almost inviting readers to go ask them.
The intro experience looks at events before students’ lifetimes, like the Roman Empire or the Civil War, so they can treat the resurrection as history too.
For a storyteller, find a history teacher or buff who tells history well; the Gospels are history told as a story that builds to Jesus’ death and resurrection.
No historical event is proven beyond all doubt; the best evidence decides. Beyond the Bible, Jewish and Roman historians and early Christian writings report the resurrection.
Rival theories (Jesus only fainted, ended in a shallow grave, or was swapped for another body) all have less evidence. Students will meet the “myth” claim in college.

forYou: If the resurrection is the thread everything hangs on, how does that shape the way I live this week?
How well could I explain the historical evidence for the resurrection to a skeptical student?
Which student might be holding back, and how can I learn what’s really in the way?
forGroup: What would be lost from Christianity if Jesus had stayed in the grave?
How do we know about events like the Roman Empire, and how does the evidence for the resurrection compare?
Which other explanation for the empty tomb have you heard, and how does it hold up against the evidence?
Where do you land on whether the resurrection happened, and what questions are still in the way?
If the resurrection is true, what might need to change in how you live or talk about Jesus?

19.title: Unit 5, Lesson 3: Deity
19.bigIdea: Don’t assume students believe Jesus is God; many admire Him as a good moral teacher without following Him as Lord. This lesson centers on who Jesus claims to be and asks students who they say He is, and why.
keyPoints: The speaker once assumed every student believed Jesus is God; a doorstep conversation with two young Mormons showed how differently people can mean “Jesus.”
John 8 is the focus because Jesus states plainly who He is, “Before Abraham was born, I am,” the claim that made the religious leaders want to kill Him.
The intro activity asks students who they think they are and what evidence backs it up; if Jesus says who He is and the evidence supports it, that matters.
Large group can include gentle, respectful interaction about the evidence for who we, and others, claim to be.
Expect the “good moral teacher” view: admiring Jesus’ teaching while refusing Him as God, because accepting Him as God means being accountable to Him.
Ask, as Jesus asked Peter in Matthew 16, “Who do you say I am?” Then ask why, and what it would take to see Him as God: not enough evidence, or not willing?

forYou: Have I assumed my students see Jesus the way I do, without ever asking them?
Where do I treat Jesus’ teaching as optional advice instead of the word of my Lord?
How might knowing where each student stands change how I pray for them?
forGroup: When Jesus said, “Before Abraham was born, I am,” what do you think He was claiming?
Why do you think so many people admire Jesus as a teacher but stop short of calling Him God?
What changes for someone if Jesus is God and not only a good moral teacher?
Who do you say Jesus is, and what has shaped your answer?
What kind of evidence would matter most to you in deciding who Jesus is?

20.title: Unit 5, Lesson 4: Apostles
20.bigIdea: The apostles saw Jesus live, die and rise, and they kept preaching even when it cost them their lives. People don’t die for what they know is a lie, so their witness is strong evidence and a call for students to live their faith beyond youth group.
keyPoints: Faith feels easy at camp or youth group among other Christians; the real test is following Jesus around everyone else once Monday comes.
Little is known of the apostles’ lives, but many died and all were willing to die for their message; in Acts 4:20 Peter and John say they can’t stop speaking of what they saw and heard.
The apostles weren’t liars: no one gives their life for something they know is made up. Their boldness shows the power of the Holy Spirit and the gospel.
Students will say others die for their beliefs too. The difference: the apostles were eyewitnesses who lived with Jesus and saw Him die and rise, not people repeating what was handed down.
Use the discussion questions on the apostles’ conviction and fate; accounts of how each died vary and online sources aren’t always accurate, but their suffering is certain.
Close the unit by looking back: miracles happen, the resurrection is the greatest, it confirms Jesus is God, and those who saw it died for it. Now how will students live?

forYou: Is my faith as bold outside church as it is among other believers?
Where do I need courage to speak about what I’ve seen God do?
How does the apostles’ witness strengthen my own confidence in the resurrection?
forGroup: How would you describe the conviction the apostles had for their message?
Why does it matter that the apostles were eyewitnesses and not just sincere believers?
If you saw something and knew it was true, how far would you go to make sure people heard it?
Why is following Jesus easier at youth group or camp than at school, and what makes the difference?
What does the apostles’ courage mean for how you’ll live out your faith this week?

21.title: Unit 6, Lesson 1: Text
21.bigIdea: We can’t show the Bible is true just by saying the Bible says so. Thousands of ancient copies show the New Testament has been passed down accurately, so what we read is what its writers actually wrote, and that is hard to ignore.
keyPoints: Articles claiming an ancient document rewrites Jesus’ story raise this unit’s question: how do we know the Bible is true, accurate, reliable and authoritative?
Avoid the circular argument, “it’s true because the Bible says so”; students need reasons from outside that loop.
No ancient text survives as an autograph (the original), only as manuscripts (copies). The question is whether there are enough accurate copies to trust what we hold.
The intro activity has students find a document that proves who they are, like a birth certificate or passport, to show how much weight documents can carry.
One Roman historian’s work survives in roughly 100 copies; the New Testament in over 6,000, and over 20,000 counting more. They agree over 95%, and no difference affects theology.
This year’s misconceptions quote real critics students may meet on TV, so teach them to check the evidence. Jonathan Morrow’s Questioning the Bible helps teens with more questions.

forYou: Have I leaned on “because the Bible says so” when a student needed real reasons?
What surprised me about how well the New Testament has been preserved?
If what Paul wrote is really what Paul wrote, what in it am I still ignoring?
forGroup: Why doesn’t “it’s true because the Bible says so” convince someone who doesn’t already believe?
What’s the difference between an original and a copy, and why does the number of copies matter?
How does the evidence for the New Testament compare with what you trust in your history textbook?
When someone says the Bible has been changed over time, how would you respond?
If the New Testament says what its writers really wrote, what does that mean for how you read it?

22.title: Unit 6, Lesson 2: Archaeology
22.bigIdea: The Bible is God’s Word, and it is also real history. Archaeology helps show it: finds connected to King David and Pontius Pilate remind us that the Bible describes real people, places and events.
keyPoints: The signature activity shows how clues like the marker, the color and the surface could date a signature, the way archaeologists date what they find.
Ancient cities were rebuilt on the rubble of earlier ones, forming layers called a tell; the deeper archaeologists dig, the further back in time they go.
A Lego model in the rubble would date its layer by when that set came out; the question for students is what biblical artifacts mean for the biblical text.
The storyteller needn’t be an archaeologist; someone who found a family heirloom in an attic works. An artifact makes a story more reliable and more powerful.
Small groups focus on the Bible as accurate history: coins point to David as king, and inscriptions show Pontius Pilate was a real governor at Jesus’ crucifixion.
Expect pushback that it’s all stories and myths and be ready to talk it through; then ask students how this evidence changes the way they see the Bible.

forYou: What have I learned these past two weeks that I didn’t know before?
Am I willing to tell students, “I didn’t know this either,” and learn alongside them?
How does seeing the Bible as real history change the way I read it?
forGroup: How can an archaeologist tell when an object was made or used?
What does it add to a story when there’s an object or artifact to go with it?
Why does it matter that people like David and Pontius Pilate were real?
What pushback have you heard about the Bible being just stories or myths, and how would you answer it?
Two weeks in, how has this evidence changed the way you see the Bible?

23.title: Unit 6, Lesson 3: Prophecy
23.bigIdea: Prophecy is trickier than history, because a fulfillment can be dismissed as coincidence or as staged. As students study Isaiah 52 and 53, expect hard questions, and meet them honestly instead of brushing them off.
keyPoints: Students can see the Bible as accurate history, but prophecy is trickier: a fulfillment can be waved off as coincidence or as manufactured to look fulfilled.
Students explore Isaiah 52 and 53 in their introduction activity, alongside the misconception, the illumination and the questions.
This may be the week students fire hard questions, especially at small group leaders. Write them down, research, and take an extra week to answer if needed.
Don’t pretend to have every answer or brush a question off; students drawing closer can still fall away if their questions are dismissed.
Address the misconception directly: it seems impossible for one man to fulfill hundreds of prophecies, and Jesus fulfilled them in ways many didn’t expect.
Many expected a political, military ruler to restore Israel; Jesus established a spiritual kingdom. That worldview shift was hard then and may be hard for students now.

forYou: How do I usually react when a student asks something I can’t answer?
Have I built enough trust that students feel safe bringing me hard questions?
Where do my own expectations of Jesus differ from the kingdom He actually brought?
forGroup: What makes a fulfilled prophecy convincing to you, and what makes it easy to dismiss?
What stands out to you in Isaiah 52 and 53, and how does it connect to Jesus?
Why do you think many people missed Jesus when He came as a different kind of Messiah?
What questions about prophecy would you like us to research together?
What expectations of God might you need to let go of to see who Jesus really is?

24.title: Unit 6, Lesson 4: Authority
24.bigIdea: If the Bible is accurate, historical and fulfills prophecy, then it has authority over our lives, so now what? This lesson helps students answer common objections and move toward appreciating, reading and following God’s Word.
keyPoints: This lesson invites a response: if the Bible is everything the past weeks have shown, it has authority over our lives. Now what?
Choose a student changed by these weeks as storyteller; a peer’s conviction can land harder than an adult’s. Otherwise, invite a graduate now in college.
Objection one: men wrote the Bible. Students ask how Matthew could record Jesus’ words exactly when most of us can’t quote a sermon we just heard.
One way to answer: if Jesus is fully man and fully God, God can also use human writers to record His words with complete accuracy.
Objection two: the Bible is just people’s ideas about God. But God showed us who He really is in Jesus, so Scripture is accurate about God, not mere opinion.
Aim for students to appreciate the Bible more, read it more and follow it better, and to talk about it intelligently with friends and in college.

forYou: Do I live as though the Bible has authority over my life, or only over what I teach?
When did I last read Scripture just to listen, not to prepare a lesson?
Which student might be ready to share how these weeks have changed them?
forGroup: After these four weeks, what conclusion are you coming to about the Bible?
How would you answer someone who says the Bible can’t be God’s Word because people wrote it?
What makes it hard to treat the Bible as having authority over your life?
What would help you read the Bible more this month?
If a friend questioned the Bible, what from these weeks would you share with them?

25.title: Unit 7, Lesson 1: Evil
25.bigIdea: Evil isn’t something God made; it is the absence of good, the way darkness is the absence of light, and it entered our world when people chose to push God out. The very fact that we can call something evil points to a standard of good beyond us, and so to God.
keyPoints: Before you start, pray for yourself, your students and your leaders: these weeks on evil and suffering may bring real pain, hurt and doubt to the surface.
Evil is approached two ways over the coming weeks, philosophical (more academic) and pastoral. Be patient: not every student will connect with both.
Evil is not a force God created. It is a privation of good, like darkness without light or cold without heat: remove God’s goodness and evil is what’s left.
Since the garden, people chose to remove God and be their own moral compass. God graciously gave us free will, and evil was the result of that choice.
Storyteller idea: someone who got lost. A compass only works if it points to something outside you; God is that external moral compass.
If there were no God, there would be no good to measure evil against. Evil exists, so a standard of good exists, which suggests God exists.

forYou: Who in my group might be carrying real pain into these weeks, and how will I pray for them by name?
Where am I tempted to be my own moral compass instead of looking to God?
How will I keep track of hard questions I table so none of them get quietly dropped?
forGroup: How would you explain the idea that evil is the absence of good, not a thing God made?
Where have you seen evil or suffering up close, and what questions did it leave you with?
What happens when people use themselves as their own moral compass? What examples come to mind?
Why might the existence of evil point toward God rather than away from him?
What questions about suffering would you most want answered in the next few weeks?

26.title: Unit 7, Lesson 2: Falsehood
26.bigIdea: Some say an all-powerful, all-good God would simply have prevented evil, but being all-powerful doesn’t mean God can do anything: he cannot lie or contradict himself. God didn’t create evil, he allows it only for a time for reasons we see in part, and he gives us real hope.
keyPoints: This lesson answers a common atheist objection: if God is all-powerful and all-good, he would have prevented evil in the first place.
In a debate, an atheist argued God would have made a perfect “God-world” of only God-like things. But then God would no longer be God; that leads to pantheism.
There are some things God cannot do, such as lie or contradict himself. Help students think about what makes God God, not trick questions like the heavy rock.
God did not create evil and is not responsible for it. He is working to remedy it, yet he still lets us have free will to make our own choices.
God has morally justified reasons to allow evil for a time. As Paul says in 1 Corinthians, we only see in part; like a parent, God may know what we can’t.
Know what your students are going through, both to pray and walk with them and to avoid touching a raw nerve. Point them to God for hope, not doubt.

forYou: What do I actually believe about why God allows evil, and where do I still only see in part?
What is each of my students going through right now that I should keep in mind this week?
When has something painful in my life later been used for good?
forGroup: What are some things God cannot do, and what do they tell us about who he is?
Why would a world where everything is equal to God mean God isn’t God anymore?
What good have you seen come out of something bad, in your life or someone else’s?
How is God allowing evil for a time different from God causing evil?
When evil seems to win, what would help you look to God for hope rather than doubt him?

28.title: Unit 7, Lesson 4: Hell
28.bigIdea: Hell is the tragic consequence of rejecting God: life with all of God’s goodness taken away. God doesn’t force anyone into relationship with him, so he honors our choice, and your job this week is to let students wrestle with that hard truth patiently.
keyPoints: The book Love Wins by Rob Bell stirred controversy; students were drawn to its idea of endless second chances and that hell isn’t really accurate.
Jesus is clear that hell exists, but it’s easy to discount because none of us wants to face consequences. Hell is not God: it’s what rejecting him leads to.
Intro experience: students describe their favorite place, then strip away every good thing about it, to sense what hell might be like.
Common grace is God sustaining every breath, the sun and the rain for everyone. Picture all of that removed: uninhabitable.
God doesn’t send people to hell; we send ourselves by not wanting him. God invites, never forces: that is love in action.
Invite open discussion rather than just pointing to the Bible. With four lessons left, take stock of where each student is now and don’t rush them.

forYou: How comfortable am I letting a student say they aren’t sure about hell without shutting them down?
Where do I see God’s common grace in my own ordinary day?
Looking back at my notes from the start of the year, where is each student now?
forGroup: Describe your favorite place. What would it be like with every good thing about it removed?
What everyday good things do you think God provides for everyone, whether they choose him or not?
Why do you think so many people would rather believe hell isn’t real?
How can a good and loving God allow hell? What makes that hard, and what helps?
What does it mean that God invites us into relationship but never forces us?

29.title: Unit 8, Lesson 1: Love
29.bigIdea: Your students now know a lot, but knowledge shared without love misses the point; as Paul says, without love it’s all for nothing. This week is about sharing faith with love and humility, listening well and building relationships, not winning arguments or counting conversions.
keyPoints: Paul says in 1 Corinthians that even if we can do amazing things, without love it is all for nothing. That’s why we keep coming back to love.
With so much knowledge gained, it’s easy to get caught up in being right, earning spiritual notches or winning arguments instead of sharing with love.
Train students to share faith in love and humility: sit back, listen, take a genuine interest in the other person, and be like Jesus.
Intro activity: students recall a time they felt loved, so they understand how others should feel when we show love.
Go a bit off script and role-play: show conversations with love and without it. Some students lean toward arguing, others toward just agreeing.
Remind them they’ll mess it up, and that’s okay: it’s a skill that grows. Focus on relationships, not conversions; our love is how some will see Jesus.

forYou: In conversations about faith, am I more focused on being right or on the person in front of me?
Which of my students lean toward arguing, and which toward just agreeing to keep the peace?
Who outside church is getting to know Jesus through how I treat them?
forGroup: Think of a time you felt really loved. What did the other person do?
What’s the difference between winning an argument and actually loving the person you’re talking with?
In the role-play, what made the loving conversation feel different from the other one?
What are some ways to show love to someone that you hadn’t thought of before?
Who is one person you could build a real friendship with this month, and what would that look like?

30.title: Unit 8, Lesson 2: Questions
30.bigIdea: You don’t need every answer to talk about your faith; good questions are the most valuable tool you have. Asking “What do you mean by that?” and “How did you come to that conclusion?” helps you understand, buys time to think, and shows real care for the person.
keyPoints: Loving people in conversation can feel terrifying, especially for introverts. Having a plan of attack helps, including when you’re asked something you can’t answer.
We feel we need every answer to convince someone. Nothing could be further from the truth: everyone gets stumped, and no one knows every belief.
This week is about the art of asking questions: not yes-or-no, but probing “why” questions that show genuine interest in what the other person thinks.
First question: “What do you mean by that?” It lets the person clarify what they believe, and it buys you time to think more carefully.
Second question: “How did you come to that conclusion?” Ask it with genuine interest, never with an attitude, so they see you want to know what they think.
Good questions are a form of love. They build a relationship, so if someone does come to Christ, discipleship can begin, not just a conversion.

forYou: When I’m stumped in a conversation, do I rush to an answer or slow down and ask a question?
Which of my students find conversation hardest, and how can I help them build a plan?
How can I model the two questions in how I listen to my own group?
forGroup: What part of talking about your faith feels hardest or scariest to you?
Why do we feel we have to have every answer, and what would change if we didn’t?
If someone says Jesus was just a good moral teacher, how could asking what they mean open up the conversation?
How can the same question sound curious or sound like an attack? What makes the difference?
Who in your life could you have a real, question-filled conversation with this week?

31.title: Unit 8, Lesson 3: Doubt
31.bigIdea: Doubt will come to your students, and doubts that are shut down rather than heard are one reason many leave the faith after high school. Make your group a place where any question is welcome and walk with students through their doubts, because God can handle all of it.
keyPoints: The speaker walked away from Christianity in high school after being told not to ask questions and to just believe, without knowing what that meant.
Many students leave youth group after high school, and unanswered doubts are one reason. More knowledge often brings more questions, not fewer.
Keep the open, authentic group you set up at the start: invite doubts about God, Jesus, the Bible, suffering and culture, and share some of your own.
Intro activity: each student writes down one question they’re wrestling with. A Q&A session lets the timid hear their question answered too.
Equip small group leaders, and remind them it’s okay to say “I don’t have an answer,” write it down, and come back with one.
Invite a storyteller who has walked through doubt; it needn’t be dramatic. Some students have small questions, others a real crisis of faith.

forYou: What doubts have I wrestled with, and which might be helpful to share with my group?
How do I usually respond when a student asks something I can’t answer?
Which of my students might be in a real crisis of faith right now, and how can I reach out?
forGroup: What is one question about faith that you’ve been wrestling with lately?
How have people responded when you asked a hard question about God, and how did that feel?
Why might working through doubt honestly make faith stronger instead of weaker?
Which topics from this year left you with more questions than answers?
When a doubt feels big, who could you talk to, and what would help you bring it up?

32.title: Unit 8, Lesson 4: Challenges
32.bigIdea: The final week wraps up the year: celebrate, take inventory of how far students have come, and prepare them for what is next. Remind them it is God who does the saving, that they will face challenges and failures, and to be faithful to the gifts God has given them.
keyPoints: This final lesson caps a year preparing students to be entirely confident and to engage their culture with the truth of the gospel.
Take time to celebrate; this has been one of the most difficult topics some students have ever dealt with in church.
Do an inventory: have students compare their thinking now with lesson 1.1, ask what questions were answered, and ask seniors if they feel ready.
Choose a storyteller who can share failures as well as successes, because students will fall flat sometimes and generally learn more from failure.
It is not us who does the saving; some water, some plant, but God causes the growth, from excavators to tree shakers.
Encourage students to be faithful to their own gifts; they will face unanswered questions and also the thrill of leading someone to Christ.

forYou: Look back at your notes from lesson 1.1. How has your thinking changed since the year began?
Have the questions you had at the start been answered? What new questions do you have now?
Are you an excavator, a tree shaker, or something in between? How has God gifted you for sharing truth?
Seniors: do you feel ready for what is next, and what would help you be more ready?
